tool.name: Vim
tool.tagline: Modal, keyboard-driven text editor available on almost every Unix machine
tool.description: Vim is a modal text editor: instead of holding modifier keys, you switch between modes and compose short commands like 'delete inside quotes'. It is installed on nearly every server, its keybindings are available in most IDEs, and fluent Vim users edit text remarkably fast.

concepts.name: Modes: insert, normal and quitting
concepts.summary: Vim starts in Normal mode where keys are commands; you press i to type text and Esc to get back.
concepts.why: Every Vim session depends on knowing which mode you are in and how to save and quit.
concepts.body:
Vim is a **modal** editor. The same key means different things depending on the mode you are in.

- **Normal mode** is where Vim starts. Keys are commands: `x` deletes a character, `dd` deletes a line, `u` undoes.
- **Insert mode** is for typing text. Press `i` in Normal mode to enter it; the status line shows `-- INSERT --`.
- **Command-line mode** starts when you type `:` in Normal mode. You type an Ex command and press Enter.
- **Visual mode** (`v`) selects text; it gets its own lesson later.

Press `Esc` (or `Ctrl-[`) to return to Normal mode from anywhere. When in doubt, press Esc.

Saving and quitting are command-line commands:

- `:w` writes the file, `:w name.txt` writes to a new name.
- `:q` quits, but refuses if there are unsaved changes.
- `:wq` (or `:x`, or `ZZ` in Normal mode) saves and quits.
- `:q!` quits and throws away changes.

The idea behind modes: most editing time is spent moving and changing existing text, not typing new text. Normal mode makes every key a one-stroke command, so you rarely need the mouse or Ctrl chords. Run `vimtutor` in a terminal for a 30-minute hands-on tour.
concepts.code:
vim notes.txt     " open (or create) a file from the shell
i                 " Normal -> Insert mode
Hello, Vim!       " type text
<Esc>             " back to Normal mode
:w                " write the file
:q                " quit
:q!               " quit, discarding unsaved changes
:help :w          " open the built-in help for any command
takeaways: Normal mode = commands, Insert mode = typing, Esc always goes back to Normal
:w saves, :q quits, :wq saves and quits, :q! quits without saving
:help <topic> opens the excellent built-in manual
pitfalls: Typing text while still in Normal mode: every letter runs a command. Press u to undo the damage.

quiz.q: You opened a file, typed some text and now want to leave without saving. What do you type?
quiz.explain: Esc returns to Normal mode, and :q! quits while discarding changes; :wq and ZZ would save.

concepts.name: Basic motions: hjkl, words, lines
concepts.summary: Move by character, word, line and file with single keys, optionally prefixed with a count.
concepts.why: Motions are half of every Vim command; fast movement is where Vim speed starts.
concepts.body:
In Normal mode you move with motions instead of arrow keys (arrows still work).

- `h` `j` `k` `l` move left, down, up, right.
- `w` jumps to the start of the next word, `b` back to the start of the previous word, `e` to the end of the word.
- `W`, `B`, `E` do the same for **WORDs**, which are separated only by whitespace (so `foo.bar(x)` is one WORD but several words).
- `0` goes to column 0, `^` to the first non-blank character, `$` to the end of the line.
- `gg` goes to the first line, `G` to the last line, `42G` (or `:42`) to line 42.
- `Ctrl-d` and `Ctrl-u` scroll half a page down and up.
- `{` and `}` jump to the previous or next blank line, i.e. by paragraph.

Almost every motion takes a **count**: `5j` moves down five lines, `3w` moves three words forward. Turning on `:set relativenumber` shows line distances so counts are easy to read off.

These motions are not only for moving. In the next lessons you combine them with operators: `dw` deletes a word, `c$` changes to the end of the line, `y}` copies a paragraph. Learn the motions well and every operator becomes more useful.
concepts.code:
w     " next word start         b     " previous word start
e     " end of word             W     " next WORD (whitespace-separated)
0     " start of line           ^     " first non-blank character
$     " end of line             gg    " first line of file
G     " last line               42G   " line 42 (same as :42)
5j    " down 5 lines            3w    " forward 3 words
}     " next blank line         Ctrl-d " half page down
takeaways: Counts multiply motions: 5j, 3w, 2}
w/b/e move by words, W/B/E by whitespace-separated WORDs
0, ^ and $ for line positions; gg and G for file start and end
pitfalls: Holding j or l to crawl across the screen; use counts, words and searches instead.

quiz.q: The cursor is at the start of `user.name = x`. Where does `W` move it?
options: To the end of the line
quiz.explain: `user.name` is a single WORD (no whitespace inside), so W jumps to the next WORD, which is `=`.

quiz.q: What does `^` do?
options: Jumps to the first non-blank character of the line
Jumps to the top of the screen
quiz.explain: ^ goes to the first non-whitespace character, while 0 goes to the very first column.

concepts.name: Entering insert mode the right way
concepts.summary: i, a, I, A, o and O enter Insert mode at different positions, saving a motion each time.
concepts.why: Picking the right insert command removes a lot of small cursor movements.
concepts.body:
There are several ways into Insert mode, each starting at a different place:

- `i` inserts before the cursor, `a` appends after it.
- `I` inserts at the first non-blank character of the line, `A` appends at the end of the line.
- `o` opens a new line below and enters Insert mode, `O` opens one above.
- `s` deletes the character under the cursor and inserts; `S` (same as `cc`) clears the whole line and inserts, keeping indentation.

So to add a semicolon at the end of a line, type `A;<Esc>` from anywhere on the line, rather than `$a;<Esc>`. That matters more than it looks: as a single command, `A;` can be repeated on other lines with `.` (covered in the undo lesson).

While in Insert mode a few keys are handy:

- `Ctrl-w` deletes the word before the cursor, `Ctrl-u` deletes back to the start of the insert.
- `Ctrl-n` and `Ctrl-p` complete words that appear in open buffers.
- `Ctrl-o` runs one Normal-mode command and comes straight back to Insert mode.

A count also works: `3ihey <Esc>` inserts `hey hey hey `. Leave Insert mode as soon as you are done typing; Normal mode is the home base.
concepts.code:
A;<Esc>         " append ';' at end of line
I// <Esc>       " comment out: insert '// ' at first non-blank
o<Esc>          " add an empty line below
Oimport os<Esc> " add a line above
3i-<Esc>        " insert '---'
S               " wipe line contents (keeps indent) and insert
takeaways: i/a = before/after cursor, I/A = start/end of line, o/O = new line below/above
A single insert command can be repeated with .
Ctrl-w deletes the previous word while typing

quiz.q: You want to add `)` at the end of the current line, wherever the cursor is. Which is best?
quiz.explain: A appends at end of line in one command (and is repeatable with .); $i would insert before the last character.

concepts.name: Operators: delete, change, yank, put
concepts.summary: Commands like d, c and y take a motion: dw deletes a word, c$ changes to end of line, yy copies a line.
concepts.why: Operator + motion is the grammar of Vim; once it clicks you can combine every verb with every motion.
concepts.body:
Vim commands form a little language: **operator + motion**. The operator is the verb, the motion says how much text.

- `d` deletes, `c` changes (deletes, then enters Insert mode), `y` yanks (copies).
- `>` and `<` indent and dedent, `gu`/`gU` lowercase/uppercase, `=` re-indents.

Combine them with any motion: `dw` deletes to the next word, `d$` to end of line, `dG` to end of file, `y}` yanks a paragraph, `c3w` changes three words. Doubling the operator acts on the whole line: `dd`, `yy`, `cc`, `>>`. A count applies too: `3dd` deletes three lines.

Some shortcuts are so common they get their own key: `x` = `dl` (delete character), `D` = `d$`, `C` = `c$`, `Y` = `yy` (in Vim; Neovim maps it to `y$`).

Deleted and yanked text goes into a register, and you put it back with `p` (after the cursor, or below the line for linewise text) or `P` (before). So `dd` then `p` moves a line down; `xp` swaps two characters; `ddkP` moves a line up.

Note that `cw` is special: on a word it behaves like `ce` and keeps the trailing space. Also, deleting with `d` overwrites what you yanked earlier, which surprises everyone once; the registers lesson shows how to get it back.
concepts.code:
dw      " delete to start of next word
d$      " delete to end of line (same as D)
c2w     " change two words, then type the replacement
yy      " yank (copy) the current line
p       " put it below the current line
3dd     " delete three lines
>>      " indent the line
gUw     " uppercase to end of word
ddp     " swap the current line with the one below
takeaways: Grammar: [count] operator motion, e.g. 2dw or d2w
Doubled operator = whole line: dd, yy, cc, >>
p puts after/below, P puts before/above
pitfalls: Expecting p to paste what you yanked after you deleted something else; d overwrites the unnamed register.

quiz.q: What does `c$` do?
options: Changes the case of the line
Deletes to end of line and enters Insert mode
quiz.explain: c is the change operator: it deletes the text covered by the motion ($ = end of line) and starts Insert mode.

quiz.q: Which command swaps the current line with the line below it?
quiz.explain: dd deletes the line (cursor lands on the next one) and p puts it below that line.

concepts.name: Undo, redo and the dot command
concepts.summary: u undoes, Ctrl-r redoes, and . repeats your last change anywhere you move the cursor.
concepts.why: The dot command turns one careful edit into many, and undo makes experimenting safe.
concepts.body:
`u` undoes the last change and `Ctrl-r` redoes it. A **change** is one Normal-mode command, or everything you typed in one visit to Insert mode, so `ihello world<Esc>` undoes in one step.

The **dot command** `.` repeats the last change. This is the single most useful key in Vim once you learn to make your changes repeatable:

- `A;<Esc>` then `j.` `j.` adds semicolons to the next lines.
- `cwfoo<Esc>` then `n.` changes the next search match to `foo` too.
- `dd` then `...` deletes three more lines.

The trick is to compose a change so it does not depend on where the cursor happens to be. `A` works anywhere on the line, `$a` is two commands and only the `a` part repeats. Using `ciw` (change inner word, from the text objects lesson) instead of `cw` repeats correctly even when the cursor is mid-word.

Vim also keeps a full **undo tree**, not just a stack: if you undo and then make a new change, the old branch is not lost. `g-` and `g+` move back and forward through all states by time, and `:earlier 5m` rewinds the buffer to how it was five minutes ago. With `set undofile` in your config, undo history even survives closing the file.
concepts.code:
A;<Esc>      " append ';' to this line
j.           " move down, repeat: ';' added again
j.           " and again
u            " undo the last ';'
Ctrl-r       " redo it
:earlier 2m  " restore the buffer as it was 2 minutes ago
:later 1m    " move forward in time again
takeaways: u = undo, Ctrl-r = redo, . = repeat last change
Design edits so they repeat well: A over $a, ciw over cw
:earlier / :later travel the undo tree by time
pitfalls: Moving the cursor inside Insert mode with arrow keys splits the change, so . only repeats the last part.

quiz.q: You ran `cwbar<Esc>` on a word. Which sequence changes the next occurrence of the search match to `bar`?
quiz.explain: n jumps to the next match and . repeats the last change (cw + typed text).

quiz.q: What counts as a single change for undo?
options: Each character typed in Insert mode
Everything since the file was last saved
One Normal-mode command, or one whole stay in Insert mode
quiz.explain: Vim groups one command or one insert session into one undoable change.

concepts.name: Searching with / and ?
concepts.summary: Search forward with /pattern, backward with ?pattern, jump with n and N, and search the word under the cursor with *.
concepts.why: Search is the fastest way to move to anything you can see or remember, and it powers substitution.
concepts.body:
Type `/` followed by a pattern and Enter to search forward, `?` to search backward. Then:

- `n` jumps to the next match in the same direction, `N` in the opposite direction.
- `*` searches forward for the whole word under the cursor, `#` backward.
- `/` followed by just Enter repeats the last search.

The pattern is a Vim regular expression: `/^def` finds lines starting with `def`, `/foo\|bar` finds either word (in Vim's default "magic" mode, `|` needs a backslash). `\<` and `\>` match word boundaries, which is what `*` adds for you.

A few options make search much nicer; put them in your vimrc:

- `set incsearch` shows the match while you type.
- `set hlsearch` highlights all matches; `:nohlsearch` (`:noh`) clears the highlight until the next search.
- `set ignorecase smartcase` makes searches case-insensitive unless you type a capital letter.

Search is also a motion, so it combines with operators: `d/end` deletes up to (not including) the next `end`, and `c/)` changes everything up to the next parenthesis. Every jump you make with search is recorded in the jump list; `Ctrl-o` takes you back to where you were and `Ctrl-i` forward again.
concepts.code:
/TODO        " jump to the next 'TODO'
n            " next match
N            " previous match
*            " search the word under the cursor
/\<id\>      " whole word 'id' only, not 'width'
d/return     " delete from cursor up to 'return'
Ctrl-o       " jump back to where you started
:noh         " clear the search highlight
takeaways: / forward, ? backward, n/N next/previous, * word under cursor
set incsearch hlsearch ignorecase smartcase
Ctrl-o jumps back after a search took you somewhere
pitfalls: Forgetting that . and * are regex characters: /a.b also matches axb. Escape them as \. when you mean a literal dot.

quiz.q: With `ignorecase` and `smartcase` set, which search is case-sensitive?
quiz.explain: smartcase turns case sensitivity back on only when the pattern contains an uppercase letter.

quiz.q: What does `d/foo` delete?
options: From the cursor up to but not including the next foo
The word foo under the cursor
quiz.explain: A search is an exclusive motion, so d deletes from the cursor to the start of the match.

concepts.name: Text objects: iw, i", a(, it
concepts.summary: Operate on structured chunks like a word, a quoted string or a parenthesised block without moving the cursor to its start.
concepts.why: Text objects make edits like 'change inside quotes' one fluent command that also repeats cleanly with dot.
concepts.body:
After an operator (or in Visual mode) you can use a **text object** instead of a motion. A text object selects a whole thing around the cursor, regardless of where in it you are. They come in two flavours:

- `i` = **inner**: just the contents.
- `a` = **a / around**: the contents plus the surrounding delimiters or whitespace.

The common objects:

- `iw` / `aw` a word, `iW` / `aW` a WORD
- `is` / `as` a sentence, `ip` / `ap` a paragraph
- `i"` `i'` `` i` `` quoted strings
- `i(` (or `ib`), `i[`, `i{` (or `iB`), `i<` brackets
- `it` / `at` an XML/HTML tag's contents or whole element

So with the cursor anywhere inside `"hello world"`, `ci"` deletes `hello world` and drops you into Insert mode between the quotes. `da(` deletes a parenthesised expression including the parentheses; `yi{` yanks a function body; `dap` deletes a paragraph and the blank line after it.

For quotes, Vim even searches forward on the line: `ci"` works when the cursor is before the first quote. Because a text object does not depend on cursor position, edits made with them are perfect for the dot command: `ciwnew<Esc>` on one word, then `*` and `.` on the next.
concepts.code: " cursor anywhere inside: print("hello world") ci" " -> print("|") change the string contents da( " -> print delete the parens and contents yi( " yank "hello world" with its quotes diw " delete the word under the cursor cit " bold -> | change tag contents dap " delete the paragraph plus trailing blank line vi{ " visually select a block's contents
takeaways: i = inside, a = around (includes delimiters/whitespace)
w, s, p, quotes, brackets and t (tags) are all objects
Text-object edits repeat well with .
pitfalls: Using cw in the middle of a word only changes from the cursor onward; ciw changes the whole word.

quiz.q: Cursor is on `x` in `f(a, x)`. What does `di(` leave?
quiz.explain: i( selects only the contents between the parentheses, so they remain and become empty.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `daw` and `diw`?
options: diw works only in Visual mode
quiz.explain: The a variant includes the trailing (or leading) whitespace, so the sentence stays well-spaced.

concepts.name: In-line jumps: f, t and %
concepts.summary: Jump to a character on the current line with f/t, repeat with ; and , and bounce between brackets with %.
concepts.why: These precise jumps make operators like dt) and cf, quick and exact.
concepts.body:
On the current line, `f` followed by a character jumps **onto** the next occurrence of that character, and `t` jumps **till** it (one position before). `F` and `T` do the same backwards.

- `;` repeats the last f/t/F/T in the same direction, `,` in the opposite direction.
- Counts work: `2f,` jumps to the second comma.

They shine combined with operators. `dt)` deletes up to the closing parenthesis but keeps it; `cf,` changes up to and including the next comma; `yT(` yanks back to just after the opening parenthesis.

The `%` motion jumps to the matching bracket: on a `(` it goes to the `)` and back again. If the cursor is not on a bracket, it searches forward on the line for one first. `d%` on an opening brace deletes the whole block including the braces. (The bundled `matchit` plugin, enabled with `:packadd matchit`, extends `%` to `if`/`endif` and HTML tags.)

A good habit: look at where you want to land, pick a distinctive character next to it, and use `f`/`t` instead of tapping `l` or `w` several times. Tools like `relativenumber` help vertically; f and t are the horizontal equivalent.
concepts.code:
" line: total = compute(a, b, c) + offset
f(      " cursor onto '('
;       " (no further '(' : stays)
t)      " cursor onto 'c', just before ')'
F,      " back onto the ',' before c
dt)     " from cursor delete up to, not including, ')'
%       " on '(' -> jump to its matching ')'
d%      " delete from bracket to its match, inclusive
takeaways: f lands on the character, t stops just before it
; repeats forward, , repeats backward
% jumps between matching brackets
pitfalls: Forgetting f/t only search the current line; use / to search across lines.

quiz.q: Cursor at the start of `call(x, y)`. What does `ct(` change?
quiz.explain: t( stops just before the parenthesis, so c changes `call` and leaves `(x, y)`.

concepts.name: Visual mode and block editing
concepts.summary: Select characters, lines or a rectangular block, then apply any operator; Ctrl-v lets you edit many lines at once.
concepts.why: Visual mode is how you see exactly what an operation will affect, and blockwise mode edits columns.
concepts.body:
Visual mode lets you select text first and then act on it. There are three kinds:

- `v` characterwise, `V` linewise, `Ctrl-v` blockwise (a rectangle).

Extend the selection with any motion or text object (`vip` selects a paragraph, `vi"` a string), press `o` to jump to the other end of the selection, and `gv` to reselect the last selection. Then apply an operator: `d`, `y`, `c`, `>`, `<`, `~` (toggle case), `u`/`U` (lower/upper), `J` (join), or `:` to run an Ex command on the selected lines (Vim fills in `:'<,'>`).

**Block mode** is the multi-cursor of Vim. Select a column with `Ctrl-v` and `j`, then:

- `I` text `Esc` inserts the text at the start of the block on every line.
- `A` text `Esc` appends after the block; with `$` first, it appends at the end of each line even if lines differ in length.
- `c` replaces the block on every line, `r` replaces every selected character.

The text appears on all lines only after you press Esc.

Visual mode is great while learning and for irregular selections, but for repeatable work prefer operator + text object (`dap` rather than `vapd`): Visual selections repeat with `.` by size, not by structure.
concepts.code:
Vjjd        " select 3 lines linewise and delete them
vi"y        " yank a string's contents
gv          " reselect the previous selection
Vip>        " indent the whole paragraph
" comment out 4 lines with a block insert:
Ctrl-v 3j   " select a column over 4 lines
I# <Esc>    " '# ' inserted on every line
" append ';' to lines of different lengths:
Ctrl-v 3j $ A;<Esc>
takeaways: v characters, V lines, Ctrl-v rectangular blocks
Block I/A insert on every line, shown after Esc
gv reselects; o jumps to the other end of the selection
pitfalls: Expecting the block insert to appear while typing; it is applied to the other lines only when you press Esc.

quiz.q: You selected 5 lines with Ctrl-v and typed `I// ` then Esc. What happens?
options: // is inserted only on the first line
// is inserted at the block's left edge on all 5 lines
quiz.explain: Blockwise I inserts the typed text on every line of the block once you leave Insert mode.

concepts.name: Substitute: :s and ranges
concepts.summary: Replace text with :s/old/new/flags over a line, a range or the whole file, optionally confirming each match.
concepts.why: Search-and-replace across a file is a daily task, and ranges make it precise.
concepts.body:
The substitute command is `:[range]s/pattern/replacement/[flags]`.

Without a range it works on the current line only. Common ranges:

- `%` the whole file, so `:%s/foo/bar/g` is the classic replace-all.
- `10,20` lines 10 to 20, `.,$` from here to the end, `.,+5` the next five lines.
- `'<,'>` the Visual selection (inserted automatically when you press `:` in Visual mode).
- `/start/,/end/` from the next line matching start to the next matching end.

Common flags:

- `g` replaces every match on the line, not just the first.
- `c` asks for confirmation at each match (`y`, `n`, `a` for all, `q` to quit).
- `i` / `I` ignore / respect case regardless of settings.
- `n` only counts matches without changing anything: `:%s/TODO//gn`.

In the replacement, `&` stands for the whole match and `\1`...`\9` for capture groups `\(...\)`. `\r` inserts a line break. If the pattern contains slashes, use another delimiter: `:s#/usr/bin#/opt/bin#g`.

An empty pattern reuses the last search, which gives a great workflow: search with `/` until the highlight shows exactly what you want, then `:%s//new/g`. After a substitution, `&` repeats it on the current line and `g&` repeats it on the whole file.
concepts.code:
:s/foo/bar/          " first foo on this line
:s/foo/bar/g         " every foo on this line
:%s/foo/bar/g        " every foo in the file
:%s/foo/bar/gc       " ...asking at each match
:10,20s/^/# /        " comment out lines 10-20
:%s/\(\w\+\), \(\w\+\)/\2 \1/  " 'Smith, Ann' -> 'Ann Smith'
:%s/TODO//gn         " count TODOs without changing anything
:%s#http://#https://#g  " alternative delimiter
takeaways: :%s/old/new/g = replace all in file
Flags: g all on line, c confirm, n count only
Empty pattern reuses the last / search
pitfalls: Forgetting g: :%s/a/b/ changes only the first match on each line.

quiz.q: What does `:%s/x/y/` (no flags) do on a line containing `xxx`?
quiz.explain: Without the g flag only the first match on each line is replaced.

quiz.q: How do you count matches of `TODO` in the file without changing it?
quiz.explain: The n flag reports the number of matches and makes no substitutions.

concepts.name: Buffers, windows and tabs
concepts.summary: A buffer is a file in memory, a window is a view onto a buffer, and a tab page is a layout of windows.
concepts.why: Working on several files at once is essential, and Vim's model differs from the tabs-per-file model of other editors.
concepts.body:
Vim separates three ideas:

- A **buffer** is the in-memory text of a file. Every file you open stays loaded as a buffer.
- A **window** is a viewport onto a buffer. Several windows can show the same buffer.
- A **tab page** is a collection of windows, i.e. a layout.

Buffers: `:e path` opens a file, `:ls` lists buffers, `:b 3` or `:b part-of-name` (Tab completes) switches, `:bn`/`:bp` cycle, `:bd` unloads one. `Ctrl-^` toggles between the current and the previous buffer. With `set hidden` (default in Neovim, but not in Vim) you can switch away from a modified buffer without saving, so most people add it to their vimrc.

Windows: `:split` / `:vsplit` (or `Ctrl-w s` / `Ctrl-w v`) split the screen, `Ctrl-w h/j/k/l` move between windows, `Ctrl-w o` keeps only the current one, `Ctrl-w =` equalises sizes, `:q` closes a window (not the buffer).

Tabs: `:tabnew`, `gt` / `gT` to cycle, `:tabclose`. Use tabs for different layouts (say, code in one, tests and logs in another), not one tab per file; buffers already give you every open file.

`:wa` writes all modified buffers and `:qa` quits everything.
concepts.code:
:e src/app.py     " open a file in the current window
:ls               " list buffers
:b app            " switch to the buffer matching 'app'
Ctrl-^            " toggle with the previous buffer
:vsplit tests.py  " vertical split with another file
Ctrl-w l          " move to the window on the right
Ctrl-w o          " close all other windows
:tabnew           " new tab page (a new layout)
:wa               " write all changed buffers
takeaways: Buffer = file in memory, window = view, tab = layout
:ls, :b name and Ctrl-^ navigate buffers
Ctrl-w + h/j/k/l moves between split windows
pitfalls: Using one tab per file and closing windows to 'close files' - the buffer stays loaded; use :bd to drop it.

quiz.q: You close a split window with :q. What happens to the file shown in it?
options: Its buffer stays loaded and can be reopened with :b
quiz.explain: Closing a window only removes the view; the buffer remains in the buffer list.

concepts.name: The vimrc: options and mappings
concepts.summary: Configure Vim with set options and your own key mappings in ~/.vimrc, using noremap and a leader key.
concepts.why: A small, understood vimrc makes Vim comfortable without turning it into someone else's editor.
concepts.body:
Vim reads its config from `~/.vimrc` (or `~/.vim/vimrc`). If none exists, Vim loads `defaults.vim`, which turns on syntax highlighting, `incsearch` and a few other niceties; as soon as you create a vimrc that file is no longer loaded, so start yours with `source $VIMRUNTIME/defaults.vim` or set those options yourself.

**Options** are set with `:set`: boolean ones on/off (`set number`, `set nonumber`, toggle with `set number!`), others with a value (`set tabstop=4`). `:set option?` shows the current value and `:verbose set option?` shows which file set it.

**Mappings** bind keys to keystrokes, per mode: `nnoremap` (Normal), `inoremap` (Insert), `vnoremap`/`xnoremap` (Visual), `onoremap` (operator-pending). Always use the **noremap** forms: the plain `map` variants re-interpret the right-hand side through other mappings and cause loops and surprises.

The **leader** key is a prefix for your own mappings. Set `let mapleader = " "` before defining mappings, then use `<leader>` in them. `<CR>` means Enter, `<C-x>` means Ctrl-x, `<silent>` hides the command echo.

Edit with `:e $MYVIMRC` and reload with `:source %`. Add options one at a time, with a comment saying why, and look each up with `:help 'optionname'`.
concepts.code:
source $VIMRUNTIME/defaults.vim   " keep the sane defaults
set number relativenumber
set expandtab shiftwidth=4 tabstop=4
set ignorecase smartcase hlsearch
set hidden                        " switch buffers without saving
set undofile                      " persistent undo
let mapleader = " "
nnoremap <leader>w :w<CR>
nnoremap <silent> <leader>h :nohlsearch<CR>
nnoremap <C-h> <C-w>h
inoremap jk <Esc>
takeaways: Creating ~/.vimrc disables defaults.vim unless you source it
Use nnoremap/inoremap/xnoremap, never plain map
Set mapleader before defining <leader> mappings
pitfalls: Using map instead of noremap, so your mapping triggers other mappings recursively.

quiz.q: Why prefer `nnoremap` over `nmap`?
options: Its right-hand side is not remapped through other mappings
It also works in Insert mode
quiz.explain: noremap variants execute the keys with their built-in meaning, avoiding recursive mapping surprises.

quiz.q: How do you see which script last set the `tabstop` option?
quiz.explain: :verbose set option? prints the value plus the file and line that last set it.

concepts.name: Registers: named, yank and system clipboard
concepts.summary: Vim stores yanked and deleted text in registers; choose one with "x, and use "+ for the system clipboard.
concepts.why: Registers let you keep several clipboards, recover overwritten yanks and exchange text with other apps.
concepts.body:
Every yank and delete goes into a **register**. Prefix a command with `"` and a register name to choose which: `"ayy` yanks a line into register `a`, `"ap` puts it.

The important registers:

- `""` the **unnamed** register, used by plain `p`. Every yank and delete writes it.
- `"0` holds the **last yank** only. Deletes do not touch it, so after `yiw` then `dd`, `"0p` still pastes the yanked word.
- `"1`...`"9` hold recent **linewise or multi-line deletes**, shifting down each time; small deletes go to `"-`.
- `"a`...`"z` are yours. An uppercase name **appends**: `"Ayy` adds the line to `a`.
- `"+` is the system clipboard and `"*` the primary selection on X11 (both need Vim built with `+clipboard`; check `:version`).
- `"_` is the black hole: `"_dd` deletes without clobbering anything.
- Read-only: `".` last inserted text, `"%` file name, `":` last command line, `"/` last search.

In Insert mode and on the command line, `Ctrl-r` followed by a register name inserts its contents: `Ctrl-r 0` pastes the last yank, `Ctrl-r /` the last search pattern. `:reg` (or `:reg a 0`) shows what is stored.

Macros, covered next, are stored in these same registers, which means you can edit a macro as text.
concepts.code:
"ayiw       " yank word into register a
"Ayiw       " append another word to a
"ap         " put register a
yiw         " yank a word...
dd          " ...then delete a line (unnamed register now holds the line)
"0p         " still pastes the yanked word
"_dd        " delete without touching any register
"+yy        " copy line to the system clipboard
:reg a 0 +  " inspect registers
takeaways: "0 = last yank, "1-"9 = recent deletes, "a-"z = yours
Uppercase register name appends instead of overwriting
"+ is the system clipboard; "_ discards
pitfalls: Expecting "+ to work in a Vim built without clipboard support; check :version for +clipboard.

quiz.q: You yanked a word, then deleted a line with dd. Which command pastes the word?
quiz.explain: Register 0 always holds the most recent yank and is not overwritten by deletes.

quiz.q: What does `"Bdd` do?
options: Deletes into register b, replacing it
Appends the deleted line to register b
Deletes into the black hole register
quiz.explain: An uppercase register name appends to the lowercase register.

concepts.name: Recording and replaying macros
concepts.summary: Record keystrokes into a register with q, replay them with @, and apply them to many lines at once.
concepts.why: Macros automate repetitive, structured edits that are too irregular for a single substitute.
concepts.body:
A **macro** is a recorded sequence of keystrokes. `qa` starts recording into register `a`, you perform the edit, and `q` stops. `@a` replays it, `@@` replays the last macro, and `10@a` runs it ten times.

Recipe for robust macros:

- **Normalise the start**: begin with `0` or `^` so the macro does not depend on where the cursor was.
- **Use searches and f/t**, not counts of `l` and `w`, so it adapts to lines of different lengths.
- **End by moving to the next target**, often `j` or `n`, so repeating it walks through the file.

If a motion fails inside a macro (a search finds nothing, `j` on the last line), the macro **stops**. That is a feature: `100@a` safely processes "all remaining lines" and halts at the end.

To run a macro over a range instead of a count, use `:normal`: `:'<,'>normal @a` runs it once on each selected line, starting at column 0. This is often more reliable than counting.

Because macros live in registers, you can edit them: `"ap` pastes the macro as text, you fix it, then `"ay$` yanks it back (without the newline). You can also define one with `:let @a = '0f=i <Esc>'`. A **recursive macro** calls itself at the end (record `qaq` first to empty it, then end the recording with `@a`), running until something fails.
concepts.code:
" turn lines like  name=Ann  into  "name": "Ann",
qa              " start recording into a
0               " normalise: start of line
i"<Esc>         " opening quote
f=              " jump to '='
s": "<Esc>      " replace '=' with '": "'
A",<Esc>        " close value and add comma
j               " move to next line
q               " stop recording
5@a             " apply to the next 5 lines
:'<,'>normal @a " or: once per selected line
takeaways: qa ... q records, @a replays, @@ repeats the last macro
Start at a known position and use f/t/searches inside
:[range]normal @a applies a macro to each line in a range
pitfalls: Recording with absolute moves like 7l; the macro breaks on lines of different length.

quiz.q: Why does `999@a` safely stop at the end of the file?
options: A failing motion (like j on the last line) aborts the macro
Vim limits macros to the buffer length
@ ignores counts above the line count
It does not; it loops forever
quiz.explain: When any command in a macro fails, the remaining replays are cancelled.

quiz.q: How do you run macro `q` once on each line of a Visual selection?
quiz.explain: :normal executes the keys on each line of the range, starting at the beginning of the line.

concepts.name: The :global command
concepts.summary: :g/pattern/cmd runs an Ex command on every line matching a pattern; :v does it on non-matching lines.
concepts.why: It turns 'delete every line containing X' or 'apply this macro to every matching line' into one command.
concepts.body:
`:[range]g/pattern/command` marks every line matching the pattern, then runs the Ex command on each. The default range is the whole file and the default command is `p` (print).

- `:g/DEBUG/d` deletes every line containing DEBUG.
- `:g!/pattern/d` or `:v/pattern/d` deletes every line **not** matching, i.e. keeps only matches.
- `:g/^\s*$/d` removes blank lines.
- `:g/TODO/t$` copies all TODO lines to the end of the file (`t` = copy, `m` = move).
- `:g/^/m0` reverses the file: each line is moved to the top in turn.

Combined with `:normal`, any Normal-mode keystrokes can be applied to the matching lines: `:g/^def /normal A:` appends a colon, and `:g/pattern/normal @q` runs a macro only where it is needed.

You can also nest a substitute to restrict it: `:g/^SELECT/s/foo/bar/g` replaces only on lines starting with SELECT. With an empty substitute pattern the inner `:s` reuses the global pattern: `:g/old/s//new/g`.

The whole `:g` operation is a single undoable change, so one `u` restores everything. Use `:g/pattern/` (print) first to preview which lines are affected, or `:g/pattern/#` to show them with line numbers.
concepts.code:
:g/console\.log/d          " delete all console.log lines
:v/error/d                " keep only lines containing 'error'
:g/^\s*$/d                " delete blank lines
:g/TODO/#                 " list TODO lines with numbers
:g/^def /normal A  # noqa " append a comment to def lines
:g/^import/m0             " move imports to the top (reversed order)
:g/^SELECT/s/;$//         " strip ';' only on SELECT lines
:g/^/m0                   " reverse the whole file
takeaways: :g/pat/cmd on matches, :v/pat/cmd on non-matches
Combine with d, m, t, s and normal
A whole :g run undoes with a single u
pitfalls: Running a destructive :g without previewing; :g/pat/ alone prints the lines first.

quiz.q: What does `:v/foo/d` do?
quiz.explain: :v is :g!, which runs the command on lines that do NOT match.

concepts.name: Vim regex: very magic, \zs and expressions
concepts.summary: Write readable patterns with \v, trim matches with \zs and \ze, and compute replacements with \=.
concepts.why: Vim's regex dialect differs from PCRE; knowing its tools turns hard refactors into one substitute.
concepts.body:
Vim's default **magic** mode treats `.` `*` `[]` `^` `$` as special but needs backslashes for `\+`, `\?`, `\|`, `\(\)` and `\{n,m}`. Starting a pattern with `\v` (**very magic**) makes every punctuation character special, closer to PCRE: `/\v(foo|bar)+` instead of `/\(foo\|bar\)\+`. `\V` (very nomagic) does the opposite, so only `\` is special, useful for literal text.

Vim-specific atoms:

- `\<` `\>` word boundaries (in `\v` mode just `<` `>`).
- `\zs` and `\ze` set where the match **starts and ends** while still requiring the context: `/foo\zsbar` matches `bar` only after `foo`. This replaces most lookbehind/lookahead needs.
- Real lookarounds exist too: `\(foo\)\@<=bar`, `foo\(bar\)\@!`.
- `\{-}` is the **non-greedy** quantifier (`.\{-}` vs `.*`); in very magic `{-}`.
- `\_s` and `\n` match across line breaks; `\_.` is any character including newline.
- `\c` / `\C` anywhere in the pattern force case-insensitive / sensitive.

In a replacement, `\=` evaluates an **expression**, with `submatch(n)` for groups: `:%s/\d\+/\=submatch(0)*2/g` doubles every number. `\u`/`\U`/`\L` change case of what follows. These combine with `:g` for surgical refactors.
concepts.code:
/\v(get|set)_\w+            " very magic: no backslash soup
/\Vfile.txt                  " literal text: '.' is just a dot
:%s/\vuser_\zsid/ident/g    " rename only the 'id' part of user_id
:%s/".\{-}"/"X"/g          " non-greedy: "hi" and "yo" -> "X" and "X"
:%s/\d\+/\=submatch(0) * 2/g  " double every number
:%s/\v<(\w)(\w*)>/\u\1\L\2/g  " Title Case every word
:%s/,\n\s*/, /             " join continuation lines
takeaways: \v very magic = PCRE-like, \V = literal
\zs/\ze trim the match but keep the context
\{-} is non-greedy; \= computes the replacement
pitfalls: Pasting a PCRE pattern like (a|b)+ into a default-magic search; without \v it looks for literal parentheses.

quiz.q: Which pattern matches `bar` only when it directly follows `foo`, highlighting just `bar`?
quiz.explain: \zs starts the reported match after foo, while still requiring foo to be present.

quiz.q: What does `.\{-}` mean in Vim?
options: Any character, as few times as possible
quiz.explain: \{-} is Vim's non-greedy quantifier, equivalent to .*? in PCRE.

concepts.name: Runtimepath, packages and autocommands
concepts.summary: Understand where Vim loads scripts from, install plugins as packages, and react to events with autocommands.
concepts.why: Knowing the load order lets you add plugins and filetype settings without mystery or slow startup.
concepts.body:
Vim finds scripts through the **runtimepath** option, a list of directories (`~/.vim`, `$VIMRUNTIME`, plugin dirs...). In each, sub-directories have fixed roles:

- `plugin/` scripts load at every startup.
- `ftplugin/<filetype>.vim` loads when a buffer gets that filetype; `indent/` and `syntax/` similarly.
- `autoload/` functions are loaded lazily the first time they are called (`foo#bar()` loads `autoload/foo.vim`).
- `after/` directories run last, to override defaults.

**Packages** are the built-in plugin manager: put a plugin in `~/.vim/pack/<any>/start/<name>/` to load it at startup, or in `opt/` and load it on demand with `:packadd name`. External managers (vim-plug, minpac) only automate this.

**Autocommands** run commands on events: `autocmd BufWritePre *.py %s/\s\+$//e` strips trailing whitespace before saving. Always put them in an **augroup** that starts with `autocmd!`, otherwise sourcing your vimrc twice registers them twice:

For per-language settings prefer `~/.vim/after/ftplugin/python.vim` with `setlocal` over `autocmd FileType`; it keeps the vimrc small. To find what is slow, start with `vim --startuptime log.txt`. `:scriptnames` lists every script loaded so far, in order.
concepts.code:
" ~/.vimrc
augroup my_au
  autocmd!                                  " clear on re-source
  autocmd BufWritePre *.py,*.js %s/\s\+$//e  " strip trailing spaces
  autocmd FileType gitcommit setlocal spell textwidth=72
augroup END
packadd! matchit           " load an optional bundled package

" ~/.vim/after/ftplugin/python.vim
setlocal expandtab shiftwidth=4 colorcolumn=89

" plugin layout:  ~/.vim/pack/plugins/start/vim-surround/
" shell:          vim --startuptime /tmp/startup.log
takeaways: runtimepath dirs: plugin/, ftplugin/, autoload/, after/
pack/*/start loads always, pack/*/opt with :packadd
Wrap autocmds in augroup + autocmd! to avoid duplicates
pitfalls: Using set instead of setlocal in ftplugin files, leaking settings into other buffers.

quiz.q: Why start an augroup with `autocmd!`?
options: It makes the autocommands run first
It removes the group's existing autocommands so re-sourcing does not duplicate them
quiz.explain: Without it, every :source of the vimrc adds another copy of each autocommand.

quiz.q: A plugin placed in `~/.vim/pack/x/opt/foo/` is loaded when?
options: When a file of type foo is opened
quiz.explain: Packages under opt/ are optional and loaded on demand with :packadd.

concepts.name: Vim9 script basics
concepts.summary: Vim9 script is Vim 9's compiled, typed scripting language for faster, saner plugins and configuration.
concepts.why: Modern Vim plugins and complex configuration use Vim9 script; it is far faster and less quirky than legacy Vim script.
concepts.body:
Legacy Vim script is interpreted line by line and full of quirks (`let`, `a:` argument prefixes, `l:` scopes, `==#` for case-sensitive comparison). Vim 9 added **Vim9 script**, enabled by putting `vim9script` as the first line of a file (or using `def` functions anywhere).

Main differences:

- Variables are declared with `var` (or `const`/`final`) and optionally typed: `var count: number = 0`. Assignment needs no `let`.
- Functions are written with `def ... enddef`, have typed parameters and return types, and are **compiled** to bytecode on first call, often 10x+ faster than legacy functions.
- Comments start with `#`, not `"`.
- Comparisons behave like other languages: `==` does not depend on the `ignorecase` option.
- Line continuation needs no leading backslash; expressions can span lines.
- Script-local by default; `export` and `import` give real modules.

Type errors are caught at compile time, so a broken function fails as soon as it is defined or first called, with a clear message, rather than half-way through running.

Neovim did not adopt Vim9; it uses Lua for the same purpose. Inside Vim, legacy script still works, and both can call each other. For new plugin code or anything with loops over many lines, write Vim9.
concepts.code:
vim9script
# ~/.vim/plugin/wordcount.vim

def CountWord(word: string): number
  var n = 0
  for line in getline(1, '$')
    n += count(line, word)
  endfor
  return n
enddef

command -nargs=1 CountWord echo $'{<q-args>}: {CountWord(<q-args>)}'
# :CountWord TODO   -> TODO: 7
takeaways: Start the file with vim9script; use var, def/enddef and # comments
def functions are compiled and type-checked, much faster
Neovim uses Lua instead; Vim9 is Vim-only
pitfalls: Mixing legacy syntax (let, a:arg, " comments) inside a vim9script file; it errors.

quiz.q: What is the main performance benefit of a `def` function in Vim9?
options: It runs in a separate thread
It is compiled to bytecode before running
quiz.explain: Vim9 def functions are compiled on first call, avoiding repeated line-by-line interpretation.
